title: Values Both Lists Share
statement:
You get two integer arrays a and b. Return every value that appears in both of them. Each shared value appears once in the answer, however many times it occurs in the inputs.

The values may be returned in any order.

examples.why: 9 appears twice in each array but only once in the answer.
Counting copies is not the point: 7 is shared, so it is listed once.

hints: For each value of a, you need to know quickly whether b contains it. What structure answers "is x in here?" in O(1)?
Put all of b in a set. Walk a, and keep the values that are in that set.
Duplicates: collect the answer in a set too, or delete a value from the first set once you have used it.

explain.intuition:
The slow part of the naive idea is asking "is this value in the other array?" by scanning it. A hash set answers that in O(1) on average, so build one from b and walk a once.

The answer must not repeat values. The neat way is to remove a value from the set the moment you report it: later copies of it in a then miss the set and are skipped automatically.
steps: For each x in a: if inB has x, push x to the answer and delete it from inB.
pitfalls: Reporting a value once per copy, like [9, 9] in the first example.
Comparing sorted arrays index by index without skipping duplicates in the two-pointer version.
Sorting with JavaScript's default sort(), which compares as strings: [10, 9] stays as it is.

solutions.title: Check every pair
solutions.idea: For each value of a, scan b. Keep it if found and not already in the answer.

solutions.title: Hash set, remove on use
solutions.idea: Put b in a set. Walk a; a value found in the set is reported and removed, so duplicates in a are skipped.

solutions.title: Sort both, walk with two pointers
solutions.idea: After sorting, advance the pointer at the smaller value. Equal values are shared; skip past repeats.
solutions.time: O(n log n + m log m)

followups: Each value should appear as many times as it occurs in both arrays (the minimum of the two counts). What changes?
b is too large for memory and is stored on disk, sorted. Which approach still works?
